newsitem.title: YUGOSLAVIA: Yugo c.bank to increase the reserve requirement.
newsitem.headline: Yugo c.bank to increase the reserve requirement.

text.p: The Yugoslav central bank said on Wednesday it would push the 10 percent reserve requirement up by the end of 1996 and adjust it to overall monetary developments despite bankers' calls to reconsider the measure.

"You (the bankers) have to look at complete measures and their overall effects, not to target just one measure and criticise it," the central bank vice-governor Ratko Banovic told a meeting of the Yugoslav Banking Association (YBA).
He said the central bank's Board of Governors discussed a further increase in the reserve requirement at its Tuesday meeting.

"We do not adopt measures in packages, we adjust one by one to respond to current monetary developments and we agreed there is enough manouevring space to further increase the reserve requirement. We think monetary development is favourable enough to justify such a step," Banovic told Reuters.
Banovic insisted the reserve requirement was a way to neutralise favourable monetary trends and reminded bankers that the reserve requirement used to run as high as 38 percent.
Bankers claimed the 10 percent reserve requrement on all deposits was a huge burden on commercial banks and that it weighed on their daily liquidity.
But Banovic rejected the criticism and said the National Bank of Yugoslavia (NBY) reinvested the same amount of dinars it had received on its special reserve requirement account.

According to some estimates, the reserve requirement means commercial banks must deposit almost 320 million dinars ($63.45 million) with the NBY. At the beginning of this week, NBY had almost 270 million dinars in its special account.
But bankers said they could not sustain such a huge payment because commercial banks have been financially exhausted.

"We pay taxes, we have to write off many bad debts and now you add to our difficulties such a huge reserve requirement, which is to be payed on all deposits at once," director of the Union Banka Dragoljub Vukosavljevic said.
But one banker was very pleased with the NBY's measure.

Milos Milosavljevic, head of the Jugobanka and president of the YBA, said: "I sleep tight since the NBY introduced the reserve requirement, and I know exactly how much money my bank has at its disposal every day."
Milosavljevic insisted the banks were neglecting a far more serious problem of not building their own reserves.
The central bank in September opted for a reserve requirement as a way to prevent the discount rate from rising.
The discount rate has been kept unchanged at 4.5 percent per month since June, and Banovic said it may retain that level until the end of 1996.
"The level of the discount rate was a signal to commercial banks to adjust their lending rates and reduce them to a more reasonable level, but that did not happen," Banovic said.
Even though the spread between the discount rate and the monthly rate of inflation is wide, it would be risky to change the discount rate at present, he said.

"But if you could reduce your lending rates, the central bank could consider slight changes in the discount rate policy," Banovic told bankers. -- Gordana Filipovic, Belgrade newsroom, +381 11 222 4254
